title: World Geography
summary: Solar system, Earth's motions and time, interior and rocks, atmosphere and winds, oceans and currents, continental superlatives and boundary lines. CGL usually asks one question here — local winds, planets, straits and 'largest/longest' facts dominate.

subtopics.title: Solar system, Earth's motions, latitudes and time
subtopics.concept: The universe is made of galaxies, and the Sun is our nearest star. Eight planets circle the Sun. Earth spins once a day and goes round the Sun once a year. Spin gives day and night. The tilt of the axis, with the yearly trip, gives the seasons.

tricks.title: Planet superlatives in one line
tricks.body: Mercury smallest and nearest. Venus hottest, brightest, spins backward. Mars red. Jupiter largest, with Ganymede. Saturn rings and lightest. Uranus on its side. Neptune farthest and windiest.

example.q: Which is the hottest planet?
steps: Mercury is nearest, but it has no atmosphere to trap heat.
Venus has a thick CO2 atmosphere that traps heat.

tricks.title: IST from the meridian
tricks.body: India's meridian is 82.5 E. 82.5 x 4 = 330 minutes, which is 5 h 30 min ahead of GMT.

example.q: When it is 12 noon at Greenwich, what is the time at 90 E?
steps: 90 x 4 = 360 minutes.
360 minutes = 6 hours ahead of Greenwich.

mistakes.wrong: Calling Mercury the hottest planet.
mistakes.right: Venus is hotter, though it is farther from the Sun.

mistakes.wrong: Adding time for places west of Greenwich.
mistakes.right: West is behind, east is ahead.

mistakes.wrong: Blaming perihelion (January) for the Northern summer.
mistakes.right: Seasons come from the tilt and revolution, not from distance.

mistakes.wrong: Treating a light year as a unit of time.
mistakes.right: It is a unit of distance.

mistakes.wrong: Saying Pluto is the ninth planet.
mistakes.right: Since 2006 Pluto is a dwarf planet, so there are 8 planets.

subtopics.notes:
### The universe and the solar system
The universe is made of **galaxies**. Ours is the **Milky Way** (Akash Ganga).

A **light year** is the distance light covers in one year. It is about **9.46 x 10^12 km**. So it measures distance, not time.

The **Sun** is our nearest star. It is about **150 million km** away. Its light takes about **8 minutes 20 seconds** to reach Earth. The next star is **Proxima Centauri**.

The solar system holds the Sun, **8 planets**, their moons, asteroids and comets. In **2006** the IAU made **Pluto** a **dwarf planet**. That cut the planets from 9 to 8.

### The eight planets
Order from the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. Memory line: *My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Noodles.*

| Planet | Exam one-liner |
|---|---|
| **Mercury** | Smallest and nearest to the Sun. No atmosphere, no moon. Fastest orbit |
| **Venus** | **Hottest** (thick CO2 blanket) and brightest. Morning/Evening Star. Rotates east to west |
| **Earth** | **Blue Planet**, about 71% water. Only known planet with life |
| **Mars** | **Red Planet** (iron-oxide dust). **Olympus Mons**. Moons Phobos and Deimos |
| **Jupiter** | **Largest** planet. Great Red Spot. Moon **Ganymede** is the largest satellite |
| **Saturn** | Rings of ice and rock. **Least dense**. Moon **Titan** is the second largest satellite |
| **Uranus** | Ice giant. Rolls on its side. Found in 1781 by William Herschel |
| **Neptune** | Farthest planet. Deepest blue. Strongest winds |

> **Tip:** Venus is hotter than Mercury, though it is farther from the Sun. Its thick CO2 traps heat.

The first four are small rocky **inner (terrestrial) planets**. Then comes the **asteroid belt**. The last four are large gas **outer (Jovian) planets**.

### Comets, meteors and the Moon
- **Comets** grow tails that always point **away from the Sun**. **Halley's comet** returns every **76 years**. It was last seen in 1986. It is next due in 2061.
- **Ceres**, the largest asteroid, lies in the asteroid belt.
- **Meteors** ("shooting stars") burn up in the air. Those that reach the ground are **meteorites**.
- The **Moon** is Earth's only natural satellite. It is about **3.84 lakh km** away.
- The Moon takes about **27.3 days** to spin once. It also takes 27.3 days to circle Earth. So the same face always points at Earth.
- It has almost **no atmosphere**. **Neil Armstrong** stepped on it on **20 July 1969** (Apollo 11), with Buzz Aldrin.

### Shape, rotation and revolution
Earth is an **oblate spheroid (geoid)**. It is flat at the poles and bulges at the equator.

- Equatorial diameter: about **12,756 km**. Polar diameter: **12,714 km**.
- Equatorial circumference: about **40,075 km**.

| Motion | Time taken | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Rotation** (west to east) | 23 h 56 min 4 s (sidereal day) | Day and night, wind deflection |
| **Revolution** | 365 days 6 hours 9 minutes | Seasons, with the tilted axis |

The spare 6 hours add up to one day. We add it as **29 February** in every 4th (leap) year.

The axis is tilted **23.5 degrees** from the vertical. It makes **66.5 degrees** with the orbit plane. On **3 January** Earth is nearest the Sun (**perihelion**). On **4 July** it is farthest (**aphelion**).

> **Watch:** Rotation gives day and night. Revolution with the tilt gives seasons. Distance from the Sun does not.

### Equinoxes and solstices
| Date | Event | Effect in the Northern Hemisphere |
|---|---|---|
| **21 March** | Spring equinox | Day equals night everywhere |
| **21 June** | Summer solstice | **Longest day**. Sun overhead at the **Tropic of Cancer** |
| **23 September** | Autumn equinox | Day equals night everywhere |
| **22 December** | Winter solstice | **Shortest day**. Sun overhead at the **Tropic of Capricorn** |

On the **equator**, day and night stay about equal all year. Beyond the Arctic and Antarctic Circles (66.5 degrees), summer brings months-long days. That is the "land of the midnight sun".

### Latitudes, longitudes and time
**Latitudes** are 180 imaginary circles (90 N + 90 S) counted from the equator.

| Line | Value |
|---|---|
| Equator | 0 degrees, the longest parallel |
| Tropic of Cancer / Capricorn | 23.5 N / 23.5 S |
| Arctic / Antarctic Circle | 66.5 N / 66.5 S |
| Prime Meridian | 0 degrees through **Greenwich** (London) |
| International Date Line | About **180 degrees**, bends around islands |

**Longitudes** are 360 meridians that join the poles. The Prime Meridian was fixed at the 1884 conference.

Earth turns 360 degrees in 24 hours. So **15 degrees = 1 hour** and **1 degree = 4 minutes**.

> **Example:** India's meridian is 82.5 E. 82.5 x 4 = 330 minutes. So **IST = GMT + 5 h 30 min**.

Places **east** of Greenwich are **ahead** in time. Places west are behind.

Crossing the **IDL east to west** (towards Asia) you **add a day**. West to east you **lose a day**.

patterns.name: Planet superlatives and pairs
patterns.howToSpot: 'Largest / hottest / brightest planet', 'Earth's twin', 'red planet', 'planet with rings', match-the-column on planets.
steps: Recall the size ladder: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, Earth, Venus, Mars, Mercury.
Fix one anchor fact per planet: Venus hottest, Mars red, Saturn rings.
Give the largest moon (Ganymede) to Jupiter and the second largest (Titan) to Saturn.
Eliminate options that break an anchor.
patterns.why: Each planet has one famous fact, and options are built to mix them.

example.q: Which planet is called 'Earth's twin' for its similar size?
steps: Venus is close to Earth in size.
It is also the hottest and brightest planet.

patterns.name: The Moon: distance, motions and landings
patterns.howToSpot: 'How far is the Moon', 'why the same face', first man on the Moon, atmosphere of the Moon.
steps: Distance is about 3.84 lakh km.
Rotation time equals revolution time, about 27.3 days.
The Moon has almost no atmosphere.
Armstrong landed on 20 July 1969 (Apollo 11).
patterns.why: The same-face fact is the most asked, and it rests on equal rotation and revolution times.

example.q: Why do we always see the same face of the Moon?
steps: The Moon spins once in about 27.3 days.
It also circles Earth once in about 27.3 days.
example.answer: Its rotation takes the same time as its revolution around Earth.

patterns.name: Equinoxes, solstices and the overhead Sun
patterns.howToSpot: 'Longest / shortest day', 'Sun is overhead the Tropic of Cancer on', 'when are day and night equal'.
steps: Solstices: 21 June (Tropic of Cancer) and 22 December (Tropic of Capricorn).
Equinoxes: 21 March and 23 September.
Match the season to the hemisphere: north summer is south winter.
patterns.why: Four dates and four Sun positions cover almost every question.

example.q: On which date is the Sun overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn?
steps: The Sun is over Capricorn at the winter solstice of the north.
That date is 22 December.

patterns.name: Rotation vs revolution and their effects
patterns.howToSpot: 'Rotation causes', 'sidereal day', 'why a leap year', perihelion and aphelion dates.
steps: Rotation (23 h 56 min 4 s) gives day and night.
Revolution (365 d 6 h 9 min) with the tilt gives seasons.
The extra 6 hours make a leap year every 4 years.
Perihelion 3 January, aphelion 4 July.
patterns.why: Questions separate 'day and night' from 'seasons', so match each to its motion.

example.q: Why is a leap year seen every fourth year?
steps: Earth takes 365 days 6 hours 9 minutes to go round the Sun.
The spare 6 hours add up to one day in four years.
example.answer: The extra day is added as 29 February.

patterns.name: Longitudes, time zones and the IDL
patterns.howToSpot: Time gap between two longitudes, IST and GMT, adding or losing a day at the IDL.
steps: Turn 360 degrees in 24 hours gives 1 degree = 4 minutes.
Multiply the longitude gap by 4.
East is ahead, west is behind.
IDL east to west adds a day.
patterns.why: One constant, 4 minutes per degree, solves every time-gap question.

example.q: Two places are 30 degrees of longitude apart. What is their local time gap?
steps: 30 x 4 = 120 minutes.
120 minutes = 2 hours.
The eastern place is ahead.

patterns.name: Comets, asteroids and meteors
patterns.howToSpot: 'Halley's comet returns every', 'largest asteroid', 'shooting stars are', comet-tail direction.
steps: Comets: tails point away from the Sun. Halley's comet returns every 76 years.
Asteroids sit in the belt between Mars and Jupiter. Ceres is the largest.
Meteors burn up in the air. Those that reach the ground are meteorites.
patterns.why: These small bodies are asked as short definitions.

example.q: Which name is given to a piece of space rock that reaches the ground?
steps: A rock that burns up in the air is a meteor.
One that reaches the ground is a meteorite.

revision: 8 planets (Pluto is a dwarf planet since 2006). Order: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, asteroid belt, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
Venus hottest and Morning/Evening Star. Jupiter largest with Ganymede. Saturn least dense. Mars red with Olympus Mons.
Light year is a distance unit. The Sun is 8 light-minutes away.
Rotation 23 h 56 m 4 s gives day and night. Revolution 365 d 6 h 9 min gives seasons and leap years.
21 June: Sun over Tropic of Cancer. 22 December: Tropic of Capricorn. 21 March and 23 September: equal day and night.
1 degree of longitude = 4 minutes. IDL east to west: add a day. West to east: lose a day.

subtopics.title: Earth's interior, earthquakes, rocks and volcanoes
subtopics.concept: We know the inside of the Earth from seismic waves, not from digging. The Earth has three layers: crust, mantle and core. Earthquakes, volcanoes and mountains show how the crust moves. Rocks are grouped into three families by how they form.

tricks.title: Discontinuity order: Come Make Good Lunch
tricks.body: Conrad (inside crust), Moho (crust and mantle), Gutenberg (mantle and core), Lehmann (outer and inner core). Repetti sits in the mantle between Moho and Gutenberg.

example.q: Which discontinuity separates the crust from the mantle?
steps: The crust-mantle surface is named after Mohorovicic.

tricks.title: Metamorphic pairs
tricks.body: Lime to Marble, Sand to Quartz(ite), Shale to Slate, Granite to Gneiss. Marble from limestone is the most asked, for example the marble of the Taj Mahal.

mistakes.wrong: Saying S-waves pass through the outer core.
mistakes.right: S-waves stop at liquids. That proves the outer core is liquid.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing Richter and Mercalli.
mistakes.right: Richter is magnitude. Mercalli is intensity.

mistakes.wrong: Calling granite a sedimentary rock.
mistakes.right: Granite is an intrusive igneous rock.

mistakes.wrong: Looking for fossils in igneous rocks.
mistakes.right: Only sedimentary rocks hold fossils.

mistakes.wrong: Placing the Moho below the core.
mistakes.right: Moho lies between crust and mantle. Gutenberg lies between mantle and core.

subtopics.notes:
### Layers of the Earth
Our knowledge of the interior comes from **seismic waves** and mining.

| Layer | Depth (about) | Key facts |
|---|---|---|
| **Crust** | 5-10 km (ocean floors), 30-70 km (continents) | Thinnest layer. Continental crust is **SiAl**, lighter. Oceanic crust is **SiMa**, denser |
| **Mantle** | Up to about 2,900 km | Mostly solid rock. Its upper, partly molten part (**asthenosphere**) feeds magma |
| **Core** | 2,900 km to the centre (6,371 km) | **NiFe**, nickel and iron. **Outer core liquid**, **inner core solid** |

SiAl means silica + aluminium. SiMa means silica + magnesium.

**Discontinuities** are surfaces where wave speed jumps. From the top down:

1. **Conrad**: inside the crust.
2. **Moho** (Mohorovicic, 1909): crust and mantle.
3. **Repetti**: inside the mantle.
4. **Gutenberg**: mantle and outer core, about 2,900 km down.
5. **Lehmann**: outer core and inner core.

> **Tip:** Moho is crust to mantle. Gutenberg is mantle to core. Lehmann divides the two cores.

### Earthquakes
An **earthquake** is a sudden shake as stored energy is released along faults.

- The starting point inside the Earth is the **focus (hypocentre)**.
- The point on the surface right above it is the **epicentre**. The shock is strongest there.
- A **seismograph** records the waves.

| Wave | Speed | Special fact |
|---|---|---|
| **P (primary)** | Fastest | Passes through solids and liquids |
| **S (secondary)** | Slower | **Cannot pass through liquids**, which proves the outer core is liquid |
| **L (surface)** | Slowest | Arrives last and does the **most damage** |

The **Richter scale** measures **magnitude**. The **Mercalli scale** measures **intensity**, which means damage.

About **80%** of earthquakes strike the Circum-Pacific belt, the **Ring of Fire**. A giant sea wave from an undersea quake is a **tsunami**. The word is Japanese for "harbour wave". The Indian Ocean tsunami came in 2004.

### Volcanoes
A volcano is an opening where magma, ash and gases escape.

- **Active:** Barren Island (India's only active volcano), Stromboli (the "Lighthouse of the Mediterranean"), Etna, and Vesuvius (it buried Pompeii in 79 AD).
- **Dormant:** sleeping, such as Fuji.
- **Extinct:** no record of an eruption.

By shape:

- **Shield:** broad, with runny lava. Example: Mauna Loa, Hawaii.
- **Composite (strato):** steep, with layers of lava and ash. Examples: Fuji, Vesuvius.
- **Caldera:** a collapsed crater.

Volcanoes cluster in the Ring of Fire and along mid-ocean ridges. **Geysers** are related. Old Faithful in Yellowstone, USA, is one.

### Rocks in three families
| Family | How it forms | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Igneous** | Magma or lava cools. Oldest, "primary" rocks | **Granite** (intrusive, big crystals), **basalt** (extrusive, ocean floors) |
| **Sedimentary** | Layers of sediment press together. **Only rocks with fossils**. Cover most of the land | Sandstone, shale, limestone, coal |
| **Metamorphic** | Heat and pressure change an existing rock | See the pairs below |

Metamorphic pairs (parent to new rock):

- Limestone to **marble**
- Sandstone to **quartzite**
- Shale to **slate**
- Granite to **gneiss**

The endless change of one rock type into another is the **rock cycle**. Coal, oil and limestone sit in sedimentary rocks.

> **Watch:** Granite is an igneous rock. It is not sedimentary.

### Mountains, plateaus and plains
- **Fold mountains:** crust squeezed into folds by plate collision. The young ones (Himalayas, Alps, Andes, Rockies) are the highest. Older folds (Aravallis, Urals) are worn down.
- **Block mountains:** land raised between two faults (Vosges, Black Forest, Sierra Nevada).
- **Rift valleys:** sunken blocks between faults (Rhine, East Africa).
- **Volcanic mountains:** built by eruptions (Fuji, Kilimanjaro).
- **Plateaus:** raised flatlands. Tibet is the highest and largest. The Deccan is another.
- **Plains:** low, flat, fertile and the most densely populated.

### Plates and drifting continents
About two-thirds of active volcanoes lie on the **Pacific Ring of Fire**.

- Fold mountains form at **convergent** plate boundaries.
- Mid-ocean ridges form at **divergent** boundaries.
- The **San Andreas Fault** is a **transform** boundary.
- **Continental drift** was proposed by **Alfred Wegener** (1912).
- The supercontinent was **Pangaea**. The ocean around it was **Panthalassa**.
- **Krakatoa** (Indonesia) erupted in 1883. **Mauna Loa** (Hawaii) is the largest active volcano.

patterns.name: Layers of the Earth and discontinuities
patterns.howToSpot: 'Boundary between crust and mantle', 'layer of nickel and iron', SiAl / SiMa / NiFe, order of the discontinuities.
steps: Write the layers: crust, mantle, core.
Attach the make-up: SiAl or SiMa, then NiFe.
List discontinuities top down: Conrad, Moho, Repetti, Gutenberg, Lehmann.
Match each name to the layers it separates.
patterns.why: Each discontinuity has a fixed position, so one ordered list answers every question.

example.q: The Gutenberg discontinuity separates which two layers?
steps: It lies about 2,900 km down.
That depth is the edge of the core.
example.answer: The mantle and the outer core

patterns.name: Seismic waves and earthquake vocabulary
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which wave cannot pass through liquid', focus vs epicentre, Richter vs Mercalli, seismograph, Ring of Fire.
steps: P fastest, S stops in liquids, L slowest and most destructive.
Focus is inside. Epicentre is on the surface above it.
Richter is magnitude. Mercalli is intensity.
About 80% of quakes strike the Ring of Fire.
patterns.why: These are word pairs, and each option swaps one word of a pair.

example.q: The point inside the Earth where an earthquake starts is called the:
steps: The point inside is the focus.
The epicentre is the surface point above it.

patterns.name: Rock families and metamorphic pairs
patterns.howToSpot: 'Marble is formed from', 'fossils are found in which rock', 'which is an igneous rock'.
steps: Sort the rock: cooled magma is igneous.
Layered deposits with fossils are sedimentary.
Changed by heat and pressure is metamorphic.
Recall the four pairs: limestone-marble, sandstone-quartzite, shale-slate, granite-gneiss.
patterns.why: Three families and four pairs cover nearly every rock question.

example.q: Slate is a metamorphic rock. Which parent rock does it come from?
steps: Slate is one of the four classic pairs.
The parent is shale.

patterns.name: Volcanoes: activity, shape and famous names
patterns.howToSpot: 'India's only active volcano', 'Lighthouse of the Mediterranean', shield vs composite volcano, Krakatoa or Vesuvius.
steps: By activity: active, dormant or extinct.
By shape: shield, composite or caldera.
Match names: Barren Island for India, Stromboli for the Lighthouse.
Krakatoa (1883) is the classic explosive eruption.
patterns.why: A short list of names and two classifications covers this topic.

example.q: Stromboli, the 'Lighthouse of the Mediterranean', is what kind of volcano?
steps: Stromboli is in Italy.
It is on the list of active volcanoes.

patterns.name: Mountain and landform types
patterns.howToSpot: 'Young fold mountains are', 'a rift valley is formed by', block mountains, highest plateau.
steps: Fold: crust squeezed. Young folds are the highest.
Block: land raised between faults. Rift valley: land sunk between faults.
Plateau is raised flatland. Tibet is the highest.
Plain is low and flat, and the most populated.
patterns.why: Each landform has one cause, and the cause names the type.

example.q: The Rhine valley and the East African rifts are examples of:
steps: Both are sunken blocks between faults.
Land that sinks between two faults is a rift valley.

patterns.name: Crust types and depth figures
patterns.howToSpot: 'Continental crust is made of', 'depth of the mantle', 'SiMa is found in', crust thickness.
steps: Continental crust is SiAl, lighter and thicker (30-70 km).
Oceanic crust is SiMa, denser (5-10 km).
The mantle reaches about 2,900 km. The core runs to 6,371 km.
patterns.why: Depth and make-up figures are paired, so learn them together.

example.q: The lighter continental crust is mostly made of which pair of elements?
steps: SiAl stands for silica and aluminium.
SiMa (silica and magnesium) is the oceanic crust.

revision: Layers: crust (SiAl, SiMa), mantle, core (NiFe). Outer core liquid, inner core solid.
Discontinuities: Conrad, Moho, Repetti, Gutenberg, Lehmann.
S-waves stop at liquid. Richter is magnitude. Mercalli is intensity.
80% of earthquakes and most volcanoes are on the Pacific Ring of Fire. Barren Island is India's only active volcano.
Igneous: granite, basalt. Sedimentary: fossils, limestone, coal. Metamorphic: marble, slate, quartzite, gneiss.
Young fold mountains: Himalayas, Alps, Andes, Rockies. Tibet is the highest plateau.

subtopics.title: Atmosphere, pressure belts, planetary and local winds
subtopics.concept: The atmosphere is a blanket of air held by gravity. It has five layers, and all weather lies in the lowest one. Pressure belts drive the planetary winds. Every region also has famous local winds and its own name for a cyclone.

tricks.title: Layer order: The Strong Man Throws Eggs
tricks.body: Troposphere (weather), Stratosphere (ozone, jets), Mesosphere (coldest, meteors), Thermosphere (ionosphere, radio), Exosphere.

example.q: In which layer do meteors burn up?
steps: Meteors burn in the coldest layer.
The coldest layer is the mesosphere.

tricks.title: Local wind by country
tricks.body: Chinook: USA and Canada. Foehn: Alps. Sirocco: Sahara to Italy. Harmattan: West Africa. Mistral: France. Khamsin: Egypt. Santa Ana: California. Loo: India.

mistakes.wrong: Placing the ozone layer in the troposphere.
mistakes.right: It is in the stratosphere.

mistakes.wrong: Calling the Harmattan a cold wind.
mistakes.right: It is dry and dusty. It is called 'The Doctor'.

mistakes.wrong: Saying the Coriolis effect bends winds left in the north.
mistakes.right: It bends them right in the Northern Hemisphere.

mistakes.wrong: Treating a tornado as a tropical cyclone.
mistakes.right: A tornado is a small land funnel, mostly in the USA.

mistakes.wrong: Putting weather in the stratosphere.
mistakes.right: All weather is in the troposphere.

subtopics.notes:
### What the air is made of
Dry air by volume:

| Gas | Share |
|---|---|
| **Nitrogen** | about 78% |
| **Oxygen** | about 21% |
| **Argon** | about 0.93% |
| **Carbon dioxide** | about 0.04% |

Neon, helium and **ozone** are traces. **Water vapour and dust** vary. Clouds and rain form around them. CO2 traps heat. That is the **greenhouse effect**, together with methane and water vapour.

### Five layers from the ground up
| Layer | Height (about) | Remember for |
|---|---|---|
| **Troposphere** | 8 km (poles) to 18 km (equator) | **All weather**. Temperature falls **6.5 degrees C per km** (normal lapse rate). Ends at the tropopause |
| **Stratosphere** | Up to 50 km | **Ozone layer** (15-35 km) absorbs UV. Calm air, so **jets fly here** |
| **Mesosphere** | Up to 80-85 km | **Coldest layer** (about -90 degrees C). **Meteors burn up** |
| **Thermosphere** | Up to about 600 km | Holds the **ionosphere**, which **reflects radio waves**. **Auroras**. The ISS orbits near 400 km |
| **Exosphere** | Beyond | Outermost. Air is so thin that satellites pass almost freely |

> **Tip:** The Strong Man Throws Eggs: Troposphere, Stratosphere, Mesosphere, Thermosphere, Exosphere.

**Ozone (O3)** shields life from UV-B rays. The "ozone hole" over **Antarctica** was first reported in 1985. **CFCs** caused most of it. The **Montreal Protocol (1987)** phases them out. The layer is slowly healing.

### Pressure belts
Four belts circle the Earth.

- **Equatorial low (Doldrums, 0-5 degrees):** warm air rises. Daily rain, calm winds.
- **Subtropical high (Horse latitudes, 25-35 degrees):** air sinks. Calm and dry. The Sahara, Thar and Australian deserts lie under it.
- **Subpolar low (about 60 degrees):** stormy meeting zone.
- **Polar high:** cold, dense, sinking air.

The equatorial low and polar high are **thermal**, made by temperature. The other two are **dynamic**, made by sinking or meeting air.

### Planetary winds
Winds blow from high to low pressure. Earth's spin bends them **right in the Northern** and **left in the Southern** Hemisphere. This is the Coriolis effect.

- **Trade winds:** from the subtropical highs to the equatorial low. North-east in the north, south-east in the south. They are steady.
- **Westerlies:** between 35 and 60 degrees. Over the southern ocean, few lands stop them. They are the **Roaring Forties, Furious Fifties and Shrieking Sixties**.
- **Polar easterlies:** from the polar highs.

The trade winds of both hemispheres meet at the **ITCZ**. It follows the Sun and gives the **monsoon** its seasonal turn.

> **Watch:** The Coriolis effect bends winds to the right in the north. It is not the left.

### Tropical cyclones and other storms
**Tropical cyclones** are violent spirals born over warm seas at 5-20 degrees latitude. The name depends on the region.

| Name | Region |
|---|---|
| **Hurricane** | Atlantic, Caribbean, east Pacific |
| **Typhoon** | China Sea, north-west Pacific |
| **Willy-Willy** | Australia |
| **Cyclone** | Indian Ocean |

A **tornado** is a much smaller funnel, seen in the American midwest. It is not a tropical cyclone. **Temperate (frontal) cyclones** form along fronts in mid-latitudes. The winter **western disturbances** that rain on north India are weak temperate systems.

### Local winds
| Wind | Place | Nature |
|---|---|---|
| **Loo** | India and Pakistan | Hot, dry summer wind |
| **Sirocco** | Sahara to Italy | Hot, red dust ("blood rain") |
| **Khamsin** | Egypt | Hot, dusty |
| **Chinook** | East of the Rockies | Warm. The "snow eater" |
| **Foehn** | Alps | Warm, dry. Melts snow, ripens grapes |
| **Brickfielder** | Australia | Hot, dry |
| **Zonda** | Argentina | Hot |
| **Santa Ana** | Southern California | Hot, dry, spreads wildfires |
| **Mistral** | Rhone valley, France | Cold |
| **Bora** | Adriatic | Cold, dry |
| **Buran** | Russia | Cold |
| **Pampero** | Pampas of Argentina | Cold |
| **Harmattan** | West Africa | Dry, dusty. Called "The Doctor" |

### Types of rainfall
- **Convectional:** daily afternoon showers of the equator.
- **Orographic (relief):** rain on windward slopes. Cherrapunji's rain is of this kind.
- **Cyclonic (frontal):** rain along a cyclone or front.

patterns.name: Composition and layers of the atmosphere
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which gas is most abundant', 'weather occurs in which layer', lapse rate, aurora, ozone, meteor placement.
steps: Recall the gases: N2 78, O2 21, Ar 0.93, CO2 0.04.
List the layers bottom up.
Place each fact in its layer before reading the options.
Remember the lapse rate: 6.5 degrees C per km.
patterns.why: Each feature belongs to exactly one layer.

example.q: The normal lapse rate in the troposphere is about:
steps: Temperature falls with height in the troposphere.
The fall is 6.5 degrees C per km.

steps: Ozone (O3) sits in the stratosphere, 15-35 km up.
It absorbs harmful UV rays.

steps: It was reported in 1985.

steps: Name the belts: equatorial low, subtropical high, subpolar low, polar high.

Deflection is right in the north, left in the south.
The ITCZ follows the Sun and links to the monsoon.

example.q: The 'Roaring Forties' are strong winds found in the:

example.q: Tropical cyclones of the China Sea and north-west Pacific are called:
steps: The region is the China Sea and north-west Pacific.
Storms of that region are called typhoons.

steps: Daily afternoon showers of the equator are convectional.
Rain on windward slopes is orographic.
Rain along a cyclone or front is cyclonic.
patterns.why: Each type has one setting that gives it away.

example.q: Which type of rainfall is seen on the windward slopes, as at Cherrapunji?
steps: Rain on windward slopes is caused by relief.
Relief rain is orographic.

subtopics.title: Oceans, currents, straits and canals
subtopics.concept: Oceans cover about 71% of the Earth. Warm and cold currents move heat around and shape coastal climate. Straits and canals are the chokepoints of world trade. Reefs, salinity and tides are the other facts the exam repeats.

tricks.title: Cold current and desert pairs
tricks.body: Humboldt gives Atacama. Benguela gives Namib. West coasts with a cold current have dry air, so deserts form.

example.q: Which cold current helps make the Namib desert?
steps: The Namib is on the south-west coast of Africa.
The cold current there is Benguela.

tricks.title: Strait to two countries
tricks.body: Gibraltar: Spain and Morocco. Hormuz: Iran and Oman. Bering: Russia and USA. Malacca: Malaysia and Indonesia. Palk: India and Sri Lanka. Dover: UK and France.

mistakes.wrong: Calling the Gulf Stream a cold current.
mistakes.right: It is a warm current.

mistakes.wrong: Saying the Atlantic is the deepest ocean.
mistakes.right: The Pacific is, with the Mariana Trench.

mistakes.wrong: Linking the Suez Canal with the Atlantic.
mistakes.right: It joins the Mediterranean and the Red Sea.

mistakes.wrong: Calling the Red Sea the least salty sea.
mistakes.right: It is the saltiest sea. The Baltic is the least salty.

mistakes.wrong: Placing spring tides at the quarter moons.
mistakes.right: Spring tides come at new and full moon. Neap tides come at the quarters.

subtopics.notes:
### The five oceans
Oceans cover about **71%** of the Earth's surface. They hold about 97% of its water.

| Ocean | Remember for |
|---|---|
| **Pacific** | **Largest and deepest**. **Mariana Trench** (Challenger Deep, about 11 km), the deepest point on Earth. Ringed by the Ring of Fire |
| **Atlantic** | Second largest. **S-shaped**. Busiest for shipping. **Mid-Atlantic Ridge** runs down the middle |
| **Indian** | The only ocean **named after a country**. The warmest |
| **Southern** | Surrounds **Antarctica**. Recognised separately in 2000 |
| **Arctic** | **Smallest and shallowest**. Partly frozen. Bering Strait joins it to the Pacific |

### Salinity
**Salinity** is saltiness. The average is **35 parts per thousand (3.5%)**.

- It is higher where evaporation beats river inflow. The **Red Sea** is the saltiest sea, at about 41 per thousand.
- It is lower where big rivers dilute the water. The **Baltic Sea** is the least salty.
- The **Dead Sea** is the saltiest water body. It is a landlocked lake. Swimmers float in it.

> **Tip:** Hot and dry with no rivers means salty (Red Sea). Many rivers and little evaporation means less salty (Baltic).

### Ocean currents
Currents are huge loops driven by **prevailing winds and the Earth's spin**. **Warm currents** flow from the equator towards the poles. **Cold currents** bring polar water back.

| Type | Current | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Warm | **Gulf Stream** and **North Atlantic Drift** | Keep west European ports ice-free |
| Warm | **Kuroshio**, **Brazilian**, **Agulhas** | Japan, Brazil, south-east Africa |
| Cold | **Labrador** | Off Newfoundland |
| Cold | **Canary** | North-west Africa |
| Cold | **Benguela** | South-west Africa |
| Cold | **Humboldt / Peru** | Western South America |
| Cold | **Oyashio** | Kamchatka |

Where a warm and a cold current meet, plankton multiply and fish gather. Examples: the **Grand Banks** (Gulf Stream meets Labrador, off Newfoundland, known for cod and fog) and the **Dogger Bank** (North Sea).

Cold currents along desert coasts dry the air. They help make the **Atacama** (Humboldt) and the **Namib and Kalahari margin** (Benguela).

### Sargasso Sea, El Nino and La Nina
The calm, weedy middle of the North Atlantic gyre is the **Sargasso Sea**. It is called the "sea without shores".

**El Nino** is an abnormal warming of the Peruvian coast. The Humboldt current weakens. It links with weak Indian monsoons. **La Nina** is the opposite. It links with strong monsoons.

### Straits and canals
| Waterway | Connects | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Suez Canal (1869)** | Mediterranean and Red Sea | Sea-level, no locks, about 193 km. Africa from Asia |
| **Panama Canal (1914)** | Atlantic and Pacific | Lock canal, about 82 km. North from South America |
| **Gibraltar** | Atlantic and Mediterranean | Between Spain and Morocco |
| **Bosphorus and Dardanelles** | Black Sea, Marmara, Aegean | Both in Turkey. Istanbul straddles the Bosphorus |
| **Hormuz** | Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman | Iran and Oman/UAE. Key oil route |
| **Bab-el-Mandeb** | Red Sea and Gulf of Aden | Djibouti-Yemen corner |
| **Malacca** | Andaman Sea and South China Sea | Malaysia and Sumatra (Indonesia). Busiest Asian route |
| **Palk Strait** | India and Sri Lanka | Gulf of Mannar lies south of it |
| **Bering Strait** | Arctic and Pacific | Russia and Alaska (USA) |
| **Drake Passage** | South America and Antarctica | Roughest waters |
| **Dover** | UK and France | Narrowest part of the Channel |

> **Rule:** Learn each strait as four boxes: two lands and two waters.

### Coral reefs and tides
**Coral polyps** are tiny animals. Their limestone skeletons build reefs. They need **warm (over about 20 degrees C), clean, shallow salt water**. So reefs grow in tropical seas and die near muddy river mouths.

- The **Great Barrier Reef** (north-east Australia, Coral Sea) is the largest living structure on Earth.
- Reef shapes: fringing, barrier and **atoll** (a ring around a sunken volcano).
- Warming seas cause **coral bleaching**.

**Tides** are the twice-daily rise and fall of the sea. The **Moon's pull** causes most of it, helped by the Sun.

- **Spring tides:** at new moon and full moon the pulls add up. The range is high.
- **Neap tides:** at the quarter moons the pulls act at right angles. The range is low.
- The **Bay of Fundy** (Canada) has the world's highest tidal range.

subtopics.title: Continents, superlatives, grasslands and tribes
subtopics.concept: There are seven continents. The exam asks which is largest, which peak is highest, which lake is deepest, and similar 'superlative' facts. It also asks the local name of each grassland and the home of each tribe. Learn these as short lists.

tricks.title: Grasslands: Pretty Pam Visits Steppe Down
tricks.body: Prairies (North America), Pampas (Argentina), Veld (South Africa), Steppes (Eurasia), Downs (Australia).

example.q: What are the temperate grasslands of South Africa called?
steps: Use the list: Prairies, Pampas, Veld, Steppes, Downs.
The African one is the Veld.

tricks.title: Lake superlatives
tricks.body: Caspian is largest (salt). Superior is largest freshwater. Baikal is deepest. Titicaca is highest navigable. The Dead Sea shore is the lowest land.

mistakes.wrong: Calling the Sahara the largest desert overall.
mistakes.right: Antarctica is the largest desert. The Sahara is the largest hot desert.

mistakes.wrong: Saying the Amazon is the longest river.
mistakes.right: The Amazon carries the most water. The Nile is the longest.

mistakes.wrong: Placing the Veld in South America.
mistakes.right: The Veld is in South Africa. South America has the Pampas.

mistakes.wrong: Naming Australia as the largest island.
mistakes.right: Australia is a continent. Greenland is the largest island.

mistakes.wrong: Saying Antarctica has a permanent population.
mistakes.right: It has only research stations.

subtopics.notes:
### Seven continents in size order
There are **seven continents**. From largest to smallest:

**Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe, Australia.**

Asia holds about 30% of the world's land and most of its people. **Australia** is the smallest and flattest. It has no land borders, so it is a "continental country".

### Superlatives the exam repeats
| Feature | Answer |
|---|---|
| Highest peak | **Mount Everest, 8,848.86 m** (Nepal-China border, re-measured in 2020) |
| Longest mountain range | **The Andes**, about 7,000 km |
| Longest river | **Nile**, about 6,650 km |
| Largest river by water volume | **Amazon** |
| Largest hot desert | **Sahara**. Antarctica is the coldest desert |
| Largest island | **Greenland** |
| Largest lake | **Caspian Sea**, a salt lake |
| Largest freshwater lake by area | **Lake Superior** |
| Deepest lake | **Lake Baikal** (Russia) |
| Highest waterfall | **Angel Falls** (Venezuela), about 979 m |
| Lowest land point | **Dead Sea shore**, about 430 m below sea level |
| Highest plateau | **Tibet**. The Pamir Knot is the "roof of the world" |

> **Watch:** Australia is bigger than Greenland, but it counts as a continent. So Greenland is the largest island.

### Highest peak of each continent
| Continent | Peak |
|---|---|
| Asia | Everest |
| Africa | Kilimanjaro |
| North America | **Denali** |
| South America | **Aconcagua** |
| Europe | **Elbrus** |
| Antarctica | **Vinson Massif** |
| Australia | **Kosciuszko** |

### Continent one-liners
- **Asia:** Everest. Baikal and the Caspian. The Yangtze. The **Sundarbans**, the largest delta. Mesopotamia (Tigris-Euphrates). The equator crosses its islands (Indonesia).
- **Africa:** The "Dark Continent". **54 countries**, the most. The Sahara. The Nile, whose White and Blue branches meet at **Khartoum**. Lake Victoria. The **Great Rift Valley**.
- **North America:** The Rockies and Appalachians. The Mississippi-Missouri system. Five **Great Lakes**: Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie, Ontario. Michigan is the only one wholly in the USA. **Niagara Falls** lie between Erie and Ontario. The **Grand Canyon** on the Colorado. **Death Valley**.
- **South America:** The Andes. The **Amazon** and its rainforest, the world's largest. The **Atacama**, the driest non-polar desert. The **Pampas**. **Lake Titicaca**, the highest large navigable lake. La Paz, the highest capital city.
- **Europe:** **Vatican City**, the smallest country. The Alps. The **Volga** (longest) and the **Danube** (most countries crossed). Norwegian **fjords**. No true desert.
- **Australia and Oceania:** The Great Barrier Reef. **Uluru (Ayers Rock)**. The Murray-Darling rivers. The Great Dividing Range.
- **Antarctica:** Coldest, driest, windiest. -89.2 degrees C at Vostok. About **98% ice sheet**. **No permanent population**, only research stations. India's are Dakshin Gangotri, **Maitri** and **Bharati**. Run under the **Antarctic Treaty (1959)**.

| Temperate | New Zealand | **Canterbury** |

> **Tip:** Fix the four classic ones: Prairies, Pampas, Steppes, Veld. The rest follow.

subtopics.title: Nicknames and boundary lines
subtopics.concept: This topic is a set of matching lists: nicknames of countries and cities, boundary lines, old and new names, and capitals on rivers. Each list is short. The exam reshuffles the options, so learn each pair firmly.

tricks.title: Sun pair
tricks.body: Rising Sun is Japan, in the east of Asia, where the Sun comes up first. Midnight Sun is Norway, in the Arctic summer.

tricks.title: Line and neighbours
tricks.body: Radcliffe split India and Pakistan. McMahon runs along the Himalayas with China. Durand divides Pakistan and Afghanistan.

example.q: The Durand Line separates which countries?
steps: Durand was drawn in 1893.
It runs between Pakistan and Afghanistan.

mistakes.wrong: Giving the Durand Line to India and Afghanistan.
mistakes.right: Today it is the Pakistan-Afghanistan border.

mistakes.wrong: Confusing Finland (thousand lakes) with Norway (midnight sun).
mistakes.right: Finland has the lakes. Norway has the midnight sun.

mistakes.wrong: Placing the 38th parallel between the two Vietnams.
mistakes.right: It divides the Koreas. Vietnam was split at the 17th.

mistakes.wrong: Putting Baghdad on the Euphrates.
mistakes.right: Baghdad stands on the Tigris.

mistakes.wrong: Swapping Rome and Paris nicknames.
mistakes.right: Rome is the Eternal City. Paris is the City of Light.

subtopics.notes:
### Country nicknames
| Nickname | Country or place |
|---|---|
| Land of the **Rising Sun** | **Japan**. It is easternmost, so it sees the Sun first |
| Land of the **Midnight Sun** | **Norway**. The summer Sun never sets in the far north |
| Land of a **Thousand Lakes** | **Finland** |
| Land of the **White Elephant** | **Thailand** |
| Land of the **Thunder Dragon** | **Bhutan** (Druk Yul) |
| **Sugar Bowl** of the world | **Cuba** |
| **Emerald Isle** | **Ireland** |
| **Gift of the Nile** | **Egypt** |
| **Playground of Europe** | **Switzerland** |
| **Roof of the World** | **Pamir Knot** (Tibet region) |
| Land of the **Maple Leaf** | **Canada** |
| Land of the **Morning Calm** | **Korea** |
| **Land of Fire and Ice** | **Iceland** |
| Land of the **Long White Cloud** | **New Zealand** (Aotearoa) |
| Land of the **Golden Fleece** | **Australia** (wool) |
| **Dark Continent** | **Africa** |

> **Watch:** Finland is the Thousand Lakes. Norway is the Midnight Sun. Do not swap them.

### City nicknames
- **Big Apple:** New York.
- **Eternal City** and **City of Seven Hills:** Rome.
- **City of Light:** Paris.
- **Windy City:** Chicago.
- **City of Canals:** Venice.
- **Forbidden City:** the imperial palace in Beijing. Lhasa too was long closed to outsiders.
- **Golden City** or City of Gold: Johannesburg.
- **City of the Golden Gate:** San Francisco.

Rome and Paris are the classic pair that options swap.

### Boundary lines
| Line | Between | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Radcliffe Line (1947)** | India and Pakistan | Drawn at Partition by Sir Cyril Radcliffe |
| **Durand Line (1893)** | Pakistan and Afghanistan | Drawn by Sir Mortimer Durand |
| **McMahon Line (1914)** | India and China (Tibet region) | Sir Henry McMahon, Simla talks |
| **38th Parallel** | North Korea and South Korea | Fixed in 1945 |
| **49th Parallel** | USA and Canada | Long straight border |
| **17th Parallel** | Former North and South Vietnam | 1954 Geneva accord |
| **Maginot Line** | France and Germany | French forts of the 1930s |
| **Hindenburg Line** | German defence line | First World War |
| **Oder-Neisse Line** | Germany and Poland | Set after the Second World War |
| **Mannerheim Line** | Finland and Russia | Finnish defence of the Winter War |

> **Tip:** Match the pair first. India-Pakistan is Radcliffe. Pakistan-Afghanistan is Durand. India-China is McMahon. Korea is the 38th. USA-Canada is the 49th.

### Old names and new names
Countries:

- Ceylon to **Sri Lanka** (1972). Burma to **Myanmar** (1989). Siam to **Thailand**.
- Persia to **Iran** (1935). Abyssinia to **Ethiopia**. Formosa to **Taiwan**.
- Kampuchea is **Cambodia**. Gold Coast to **Ghana** (1957). Rhodesia to **Zimbabwe** (1980).
- Nyasaland to **Malawi**. Dutch East Indies to **Indonesia**. East Pakistan to **Bangladesh** (1971).

Cities:

- Constantinople to **Istanbul**. Peking to **Beijing**. Rangoon to **Yangon**.
- Saigon to **Ho Chi Minh City**. Batavia to **Jakarta**. Leningrad to **St Petersburg**.
- Bombay to Mumbai, Madras to Chennai, Calcutta to Kolkata.

### Capitals and their rivers
| Capital | River | Capital | River |
|---|---|---|---|
| London | Thames | Cairo | Nile |
| Paris | Seine | Baghdad | **Tigris** |
| Rome | Tiber | Khartoum | Blue and White Nile meet |
| Moscow | Moskva | Delhi | Yamuna |
| Berlin | Spree | Dhaka | Buriganga |

Baghdad is on the **Tigris**, not the Euphrates. Khartoum is at the Nile confluence. Downstream, the Danube capitals run Vienna, Budapest, Belgrade.

example.q: Which is the largest planet of the solar system?
example.solution:
The big gas planets are Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune
Jupiter is the biggest of them
Its moon Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "Two places 15° apart: what is the time difference?"

Places in the east are ahead; places in the west are behind.

example.q: What is the time difference between two places 15° of longitude apart?
example.solution:
15 × 4 = 60 minutes
60 minutes = 1 hour
The eastern place is ahead
**1 hour**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "Which boundary separates the mantle and the core?" or "which wave cannot pass through liquid?"
pyqPatterns.approach:
Moho separates the crust and the mantle. Gutenberg separates the mantle and the core.
S-waves cannot pass through liquid.

example.q: Which discontinuity separates the mantle from the core?
example.solution:
Earth's layers from the top: crust, mantle, core
The crust-mantle boundary is Moho
The mantle-core boundary is at about 2,900 km depth and is called Gutenberg
**Gutenberg discontinuity**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "Weather occurs in which layer?" or "ozone layer is in which layer?"

example.q: In which layer of the atmosphere is the ozone layer found?
example.solution:
The layers go up from the ground
The 1st layer is the troposphere, where weather happens
The 2nd layer holds the ozone layer, the stratosphere
**Stratosphere**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "Chinook / Loo / Mistral is a wind of which region?"

example.q: The Chinook, called the "snow eater", blows down which mountains?
example.solution:
The Chinook is a warm, dry wind
It blows down the eastern slopes of the Rockies
It melts snow fast, so it is called the "snow eater"
**Rockies**

example.q: The Suez Canal joins the Mediterranean Sea to which sea?

The Suez Canal is in Egypt
It links the Mediterranean with one other sea

So the answer is the **Red Sea**

example.q: Which cold current along South America's west coast is linked with the Atacama desert?
example.solution:
The current flows along the coast of Peru and Chile
It is cold, so the coast gets little rain
This is why the Atacama is so dry

solvedExamples.q: Which planet is known as the 'Earth's twin' and is also the hottest planet of the solar system?
solvedExamples.solution: **Venus** has nearly the same size and mass as the Earth (hence 'twin'). Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere causes a runaway greenhouse effect, making it hotter than Mercury even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Greenhouse beats distance: Venus > Mercury in temperature.

solvedExamples.q: If it is 10:00 a.m. at a place on 15°W, what is the local time at a place on 75°E?
solvedExamples.solution: Longitude difference = 15 + 75 = **90°** (they are on opposite sides of Greenwich, so add). Time difference = 90 × 4 = 360 min = **6 hours**. The eastern place is ahead: 10:00 a.m. + 6 h = **4:00 p.m.**
solvedExamples.shortcut: Opposite sides → add degrees; divide by 15 for hours: 90/15 = 6 h.

solvedExamples.q: The Chinook, a warm and dry wind known as the 'snow eater', blows along the eastern slopes of the:
solvedExamples.solution: The **Chinook** descends the eastern (leeward) slopes of the **Rocky Mountains** in the USA and Canada. It warms by compression and melts snow quickly. The similar wind of the **Alps** is the **Foehn**.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Chinook — a Native American name → North America → Rockies.

solvedExamples.q: The Strait of Hormuz connects which two water bodies?
options: Red Sea and Gulf of Aden
Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman
Black Sea and Sea of Marmara
solvedExamples.solution: The **Strait of Hormuz** lies between **Iran** and **Oman** and links the **Persian Gulf** to the **Gulf of Oman** (Arabian Sea) — a key oil route. Red Sea–Gulf of Aden is Bab-el-Mandeb; Black Sea–Marmara is Bosphorus; Mediterranean–Atlantic is Gibraltar.

practice.q: Which planet has the largest moon of the solar system, Ganymede?
practice.solution: **Ganymede**, a moon of **Jupiter**, is the largest natural satellite in the solar system — bigger than Mercury. Saturn's largest moon is Titan.

practice.q: On which date does the Northern Hemisphere experience its longest day?
practice.solution: On **21 June** (summer solstice) the Sun is overhead at the **Tropic of Cancer**, giving the Northern Hemisphere its longest day. 21 March and 23 September are equinoxes; 22 December is the winter solstice.

practice.q: A traveller crossing the International Date Line from east to west (for example, from the USA to Japan) will:
options: gain one day on the calendar
practice.solution: Moving **westward** across the IDL the calendar jumps **one day ahead** (e.g. Monday becomes Tuesday). Moving eastward the date goes back one day, so a day is repeated.
practice.shortcut: West-bound = skip ahead a day; East-bound = repeat a day.

practice.q: The boundary between the Earth's crust and the mantle is called the:
practice.solution: The **Mohorovičić (Moho) discontinuity** separates the crust from the mantle. Gutenberg separates mantle and core, Lehmann separates outer and inner core, and Conrad lies within the crust.
practice.shortcut: 'Come Make Good Lunch' — Moho is second.

practice.q: Marble is a metamorphic rock formed from which rock?
practice.solution: Heat and pressure recrystallise **limestone** (calcium carbonate) into **marble**. Sandstone becomes quartzite, shale becomes slate and granite becomes gneiss.

practice.q: Which seismic waves cannot travel through liquids?
practice.solution: **S-waves** (secondary, transverse) cannot pass through liquids. Their absence beyond about 103° from the epicentre (the S-wave shadow zone) showed that the **outer core is liquid**. P-waves pass through all states.

practice.q: The ozone layer, which absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation, lies mainly in the:
practice.solution: The **ozone layer** lies in the **stratosphere** (roughly 15–35 km). The troposphere has weather, the mesosphere burns meteors and the thermosphere contains the ionosphere.

practice.q: The dry, dusty Harmattan wind, locally called 'The Doctor', blows over:
practice.solution: The **Harmattan** blows from the Sahara over **West Africa** towards the Guinea coast. Its dryness brings relief from humid heat, hence 'The Doctor'. Egypt has the Khamsin, France the Mistral and California the Santa Ana.

practice.q: Tropical cyclones in the north-west Pacific Ocean (near China, Japan and the Philippines) are called:
practice.solution: They are **typhoons**. The same kind of storm is a **hurricane** in the Atlantic/Caribbean and a **cyclone** in the Indian Ocean. A tornado is a small land funnel, not a tropical cyclone.

practice.q: Which of the following is a cold ocean current?
practice.solution: The **Humboldt (Peru) Current** flows north along the west coast of South America and is **cold**; it supports rich fisheries and helps create the Atacama desert. Gulf Stream, Kuroshio and Agulhas are warm currents.
practice.shortcut: Cold currents hug western coasts in the subtropics.

practice.q: The Strait of Gibraltar separates which two countries?
practice.solution: The **Strait of Gibraltar** lies between **Spain** (Europe) and **Morocco** (Africa) and links the Mediterranean Sea with the Atlantic Ocean.

practice.q: Which is the deepest lake in the world?
practice.solution: **Lake Baikal** in Siberia (Russia) is the deepest and oldest lake and holds the largest volume of fresh water. The Caspian is the largest lake by area, Superior the largest freshwater lake by area and Titicaca the highest navigable lake.

practice.q: The temperate grasslands of Argentina are known as:
practice.solution: The **Pampas** are the temperate grasslands of **Argentina** (and Uruguay). Prairies are in North America, Steppes in Eurasia and Downs in Australia.

practice.q: Which country is known as the 'Land of the Midnight Sun'?
practice.solution: **Norway** lies largely north of the Arctic Circle, where the Sun stays visible at midnight in summer. Finland is the 'Land of Thousand Lakes' and Japan the 'Land of the Rising Sun'.

practice.q: The Durand Line forms the boundary between:
practice.solution: The **Durand Line** (1893, drawn by Sir Mortimer Durand) marks the **Pakistan–Afghanistan** border. India–China is the McMahon Line and India–Pakistan is the Radcliffe Line.

practice.q: Which planet of the solar system is the **hottest**?
practice.solution: **Venus** is the hottest planet because its thick carbon-dioxide atmosphere traps heat (runaway greenhouse effect); its surface is hotter even than Mercury's.
practice.shortcut: Closest to the Sun is Mercury; hottest is Venus.

practice.q: Which planet is called the **Morning Star** and the **Evening Star**?
practice.solution: **Venus** is the brightest planet and, seen near the horizon before sunrise or after sunset, was called the Morning and Evening Star.

practice.q: Which planet rotates on its axis from **east to west**, opposite to most planets?
practice.solution: **Venus** spins retrograde - east to west - so its Sun rises in the west. Uranus rolls on its side; the rest rotate west to east.

practice.q: Which planet is the **least dense** - so light it would float on water?
practice.solution: **Saturn's** density (about 0.7 g/cm3) is less than that of water. Its famous rings are pieces of ice and rock.

practice.q: The largest volcano of the solar system, **Olympus Mons**, is on which planet?
practice.solution: **Olympus Mons** rises on **Mars**, the 'Red Planet' (its colour comes from iron-oxide dust). Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos.

practice.q: The average distance of the Moon from the Earth is about:
practice.solution: The Moon is about **3,84,000 km (3.84 lakh km)** away - light takes about 1.3 seconds to cross that gap.

practice.q: The Moon has practically no atmosphere because:
options: It is too far from the Sun
Its gravity is too weak to hold gases
practice.solution: The Moon's small mass gives it very weak gravity, so it cannot retain an atmosphere; hence the sky is black even in daytime and astronauts' footprints last for ages.

practice.q: Who was the first human being to walk on the Moon, in July 1969?
practice.solution: **Neil Armstrong** of Apollo 11 stepped onto the Moon on **20 July 1969** in the Sea of Tranquility; Buzz Aldrin followed, while Michael Collins orbited above.

practice.q: The Sun is vertically overhead the **Tropic of Cancer** on:
practice.solution: On **21 June**, the summer solstice, the Sun stands overhead the Tropic of Cancer and the Northern Hemisphere has its longest day.

practice.q: The Northern Hemisphere has its **shortest day** on:
practice.solution: On **22 December** (winter solstice) the Sun is overhead the Tropic of Capricorn; the north has its shortest day while the south enjoys midsummer.

practice.q: On the **equator**, the length of day and night through the year is:
practice.solution: The circle of illumination always bisects the equator, so days and nights stay roughly equal there; the contrast grows towards the poles.

practice.q: Day and night on the Earth are caused by:
practice.solution: The Earth's **rotation** on its axis once in about 24 hours turns one half towards the Sun (day) and the other away (night). Revolution causes the seasons.

practice.q: The exact time the Earth takes for one rotation with respect to the stars (the sidereal day) is:
practice.solution: The **sidereal day is 23 h 56 min 4 s**; the solar day we use averages 24 hours because the Earth also moves along its orbit.

practice.q: Earth is **nearest** to the Sun (perihelion) on:
practice.solution: **Perihelion falls on 3 January** (about 147 million km); aphelion, the farthest point (152 million km), comes on 4 July - so the north's winter happens near the nearest point.

practice.q: Indian Standard Time is ahead of GMT by:
practice.solution: IST is based on the 82.5 E meridian: 82.5 x 4 minutes = 330 minutes = **5 h 30 min** ahead of Greenwich.

practice.q: A traveller flying **east across the International Date Line** (from Asia towards America) must:
options: Add one day to the date
practice.solution: Across the IDL: going **east, lose a day**; going west (towards Asia), add a day. The line bends around islands so that no country is split into two dates.

practice.q: If the local time of place A (60 E) is 12 noon, what is the local time of place B (90 E)?
practice.solution: B lies 30 degrees **east** of A, so it is ahead: 30 x 4 min = 120 min = 2 hours. Local time at B = 12 noon + 2 h = **2 p.m.**

practice.q: Which layer of the Earth is made mainly of **nickel and iron**?
practice.solution: The **core (NiFe)** is iron-nickel; the outer core is liquid and the inner core solid. SiAl/SiMa describe the crust; the mantle is iron-magnesium silicate rock.

practice.q: The **Mohorovicic (Moho) discontinuity** separates:
practice.solution: **Moho = crust-mantle boundary** (1909). Gutenberg separates mantle and outer core; Conrad lies within the crust; Lehmann splits the two cores.

practice.q: Which of the following discontinuities lies **within the mantle**?
practice.solution: **Repetti** divides the upper and lower mantle. Conrad is inside the crust, Moho is crust-mantle, Gutenberg is mantle-core, Lehmann is between the cores.

practice.q: Earthquake waves are recorded by an instrument called the:
practice.solution: A **seismograph** records the shock waves. Richter and Mercalli are scales for magnitude and damage, not instruments.

practice.q: The energy released by an earthquake (its magnitude) is measured on the:
practice.solution: **Richter scale** = magnitude (energy). **Mercalli** = intensity of damage at a place. (Fujita rates tornadoes; Beaufort rates wind.)

practice.q: Which seismic waves are the **last to arrive** but cause the greatest destruction?
practice.solution: **L-waves** travel along the surface, arrive last, and shake buildings the most. P-waves are fastest; S-waves cannot cross liquids.

practice.q: About what share of the world's earthquakes occurs in the Circum-Pacific 'Ring of Fire'?
practice.solution: Roughly **80%** of the world's largest earthquakes - and most volcanoes - occur along the ring of subduction zones fringing the Pacific Ocean.

practice.q: Fossils of plants and animals are found only in which type of rock?
practice.solution: Only **sedimentary rocks** form in layers at the surface, where living remains can be buried; heat and pressure in other rocks destroy them.

practice.q: Quartzite is the metamorphic form of which rock?
practice.solution: **Sandstone - quartzite**. Limestone turns to marble, shale to slate, granite to gneiss.

practice.q: Granite and basalt are examples of which family of rocks?
practice.solution: **Igneous** rocks cool from magma or lava: granite (intrusive/plutonic, large crystals) and basalt (extrusive/volcanic, as on ocean floors and the Deccan).

practice.q: Which of the following is correctly matched?
practice.solution: **Slate comes from shale.** Marble is from limestone, gneiss from granite, quartzite from sandstone - the classic four pairs.

practice.q: **Barren Island**, India's only active volcano, lies in which water body?
practice.solution: **Barren Island** in the **Andaman Sea** (Andaman & Nicobar Islands) erupted again from 1991 onwards; nearby Narcondam is dormant.

practice.q: Which of these is a **shield volcano** with broad, gently sloping sides of fluid lava?
practice.solution: **Mauna Loa** (Hawaii) is the classic shield volcano. Fuji and Vesuvius are steep composite (strato) volcanoes built of alternating lava and ash.

practice.q: Mount Vesuvius, whose 79 AD eruption buried the Roman town of Pompeii, is located in:
practice.solution: **Vesuvius** stands near Naples, **Italy**; Pompeii lay under its ash. Etna (Sicily) and Stromboli are Italy's other famous volcanoes.

practice.q: The Himalayas, the Alps and the Andes are examples of:
practice.solution: They rose in the recent geological past where plates collided, so they are **young fold mountains** - the highest ranges on Earth. The Aravallis are old, worn folds.

practice.q: The Vosges and the Black Forest, raised between two faults, are examples of:
practice.solution: **Block mountains** (horsts) rise between parallel faults while rift valleys (graben) sink - as on either side of the Rhine rift.

practice.q: Which is the highest and largest plateau in the world?
practice.solution: The **Tibetan Plateau** ('the roof of the world', averaging over 4,500 m) is the highest and largest; the Pamir Knot, where ranges meet, lies at its western end.

practice.q: Which is the **most abundant gas** in the Earth's atmosphere?
practice.solution: **Nitrogen makes up about 78%** of dry air, oxygen about 21%, argon 0.93% and CO2 about 0.04%.

practice.q: Clouds, rain and storms - all weather - are confined to which layer?
practice.solution: Almost all water vapour lies in the **troposphere**, the lowest layer (8-18 km), so all weather happens there. Jet aircraft cruise above it, in the calm stratosphere.

practice.q: **Meteors** ('shooting stars') mostly burn up in which layer of the atmosphere?
practice.solution: The **mesosphere** (up to 80-85 km) is dense enough to burn incoming meteors by friction - and it is also the coldest layer (about -90 degrees C).

practice.q: The chemical formula of **ozone** is:
practice.solution: **Ozone is O3** - three oxygen atoms per molecule; it forms a shield in the stratosphere that absorbs ultraviolet rays.

practice.q: The **Montreal Protocol (1987)** is an international agreement to:
practice.solution: It phases out **CFCs** and related chemicals that destroy stratospheric ozone - the main cause of the ozone hole over Antarctica.

practice.q: Which atmospheric layer contains the ozone layer that absorbs ultraviolet radiation, and is therefore favoured by jet aircraft?
practice.solution: The **stratosphere** holds the ozone layer (15-35 km) and its calm, cloudless air suits long-haul flights.

practice.q: The equatorial belt of calm, rising air with daily convectional rains is called the:
practice.solution: The **Doldrums** (equatorial low, 0-5 degrees) are hot, humid and windless - sailing ships were often becalmed there. The subtropical high is the 'horse latitudes' belt.

practice.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, the **north-east trade winds** blow:
options: From the equatorial low towards the subtropical high
From west to east at 35-60 degrees
From the subtropical high towards the equatorial low
practice.solution: Trades flow out of the subtropical highs towards the Doldrums, deflected to become **north-east trades** in the north and **south-east trades** in the south.

practice.q: Winds are deflected to the **right of their path** in the Northern Hemisphere because of:
practice.solution: The **Coriolis effect** of the Earth's spin bends moving air right in the north and left in the south - shaping the trades, westerlies and cyclone spirals.

practice.q: A **tropical cyclone** occurring in the **Atlantic Ocean and Caribbean Sea** is called a:
practice.solution: Atlantic and east-Pacific storms are **hurricanes**; typhoon is the name in the north-west Pacific, willy-willy off Australia, and simply cyclone in the Indian Ocean.

practice.q: Which of the following is **NOT** a tropical cyclone?
practice.solution: A **tornado** is a narrow, violently rotating funnel typical of the American midwest - quite different from the broad warm-sea tropical cyclones.

practice.q: The winter rains of Punjab and Haryana, useful for the rabi crop, come from which weather system?
options: Tropical cyclones of the Bay of Bengal
practice.solution: **Western disturbances** are weak temperate (frontal) cyclones travelling from the Mediterranean region; they bring gentle winter rain to north-west India and snow to the hills.

practice.q: The warm, dry **'snow eater'** wind that blows down the eastern slopes of the Rockies in North America is the:
practice.solution: The **Chinook** melts the winter snow on the prairie side of the Rockies overnight. The Foehn is its Alpine counterpart.

practice.q: The **Mistral**, a cold, dry wind that chills the Rhone valley in winter, blows over:
practice.solution: The **Mistral** funnels down the Rhone valley in southern **France** towards the Mediterranean; the Bora is its cold counterpart on the Adriatic.

practice.q: The **Sirocco**, a hot wind that carries red dust from the Sahara and sometimes drops 'blood rain' on southern Europe, blows towards:
practice.solution: The **Sirocco** picks up heat and red dust crossing the Sahara and reaches Sicily and southern Italy. The Harmattan blows westward across West Africa.

practice.q: Which is the **largest ocean** in the world?
practice.solution: The **Pacific** is the largest and deepest ocean - it covers more area than all the land put together and holds the Mariana Trench.

practice.q: The Mariana Trench, the deepest known point of the oceans, lies in which ocean?
practice.solution: The **Mariana Trench** (Challenger Deep, about 11 km deep) lies in the western **Pacific**, near the Mariana Islands.

practice.q: Which ocean is the **only one named after a country**?
practice.solution: The **Indian Ocean** takes its name from India; it is the third largest and the warmest ocean.

practice.q: Which of these oceans was designated as a separate ocean most recently (in 2000), encircling Antarctica?
practice.solution: The **Southern Ocean** (Antarctic Ocean), circumscribing Antarctica, was recognised separately around **2000**; the Arctic remains the smallest ocean.

practice.q: Which of the following is a **warm ocean current**?
practice.solution: The **Gulf Stream** is a warm current of the Atlantic; Labrador, Canary and Benguela are all cold currents.

practice.q: Icebergs off Newfoundland and the fog over the Grand Banks are caused mainly by the meeting of:
practice.solution: The warm **Gulf Stream** meets the cold **Labrador current** off Newfoundland - fog and icebergs at the Grand Banks, plus rich fishing grounds where plankton thrives.

practice.q: The Atacama desert of South America owes its extreme dryness partly to the cold current flowing along its coast, called the:
practice.solution: The cold **Humboldt (Peru) current** cools the air, so little rain falls - making the Atacama. Its warm-water reversal is **El Nino**.

practice.q: The meeting of which two currents creates the rich Dogger Bank fishing ground of the North Sea?
options: North Atlantic Drift and Arctic cold current
practice.solution: Where the warm **North Atlantic Drift** meets cold Arctic water over the submerged moraine of the **Dogger Bank**, plankton abounds - hence herring and cod. Grand Banks is its Atlantic twin.

practice.q: The Bosphorus and the Dardanelles straits, connecting the Black Sea with the Mediterranean, lie in which country?
practice.solution: Both straits pass through **Turkey** - the Bosphorus at Istanbul (Sea of Marmara between them) and the Dardanelles towards the Aegean.

practice.q: Which strait separates India from Sri Lanka?
practice.solution: The **Palk Strait** lies between India (Tamil Nadu) and northern Sri Lanka; the Gulf of Mannar is south of it, with Adam's Bridge shoals in between.

practice.q: Which strait connects the **Red Sea** with the **Gulf of Aden** and lies between Yemen and Djibouti?
practice.solution: **Bab-el-Mandeb** ('Gate of Tears') guards the southern entrance to the Red Sea; Hormuz guards the Persian Gulf, Malacca the Andaman Sea-China Sea route.

practice.q: The Panama Canal connects the Atlantic Ocean with the:
practice.solution: The **Panama Canal** (opened 1914) cuts across the Isthmus of Panama between the Atlantic (Caribbean) and the **Pacific**; it is a lock canal.

practice.q: Which statement about the **Suez Canal** is correct?
options: It is in Panama and has six locks
It is in Egypt, is a sea-level canal without locks
It connects the Atlantic and Pacific oceans
practice.solution: The **Suez Canal** (1869, Egypt) runs sea-level from Port Said to Suez - **no locks** - and shortens the Europe-Asia route. Panama (1914) is the lock canal.

practice.q: The Kiel Canal connects the:
practice.solution: The **Kiel Canal** (Germany) joins the North Sea with the Baltic - a favourite distractor alongside Suez and Panama.

practice.q: The average salinity of ocean water is about:
practice.solution: Ocean water averages **35 per mille** (about 3.5% salt). The Red Sea reaches about 41; the Baltic may fall below 10.

practice.q: Corals cannot grow in which of the following conditions?
options: Deep water beyond the sunlight zone
Salt water of normal ocean salinity
practice.solution: Corals need **shallow, sunlit, clean, warm (over 20 C) salt water** - they live in symbiosis with algae that require light. Cold or muddy water kills them.

practice.q: The Great Barrier Reef, the largest coral reef of the world, lies off the coast of:
practice.solution: The **Great Barrier Reef** stretches about 2,000 km off Queensland, north-east **Australia** - the largest structure built by living organisms.

practice.q: **Spring tides**, the highest tides of the month, occur when:
options: The Moon is in its first quarter
The Sun, Moon and Earth are in a straight line (new or full moon)
The Moon is farthest from Earth
Strong winds pile water on the shore
practice.solution: At new and full moon the Sun's and Moon's pulls combine - spring tides; at the quarters (neap tides) they work at right angles and the range is least. The Bay of Fundy (Canada) has the world's highest tidal range.

practice.q: The longest river in the world is generally taken to be the:
practice.solution: The **Nile (about 6,650 km)** is the longest; the **Amazon** is the largest by volume of water. The Yangtze is the longest of Asia.

practice.q: The highest peak of **South America** is:
practice.solution: **Aconcagua** (Argentina, about 6,960 m) tops South America. Vinson - Antarctica, Denali - North America, Elbrus - Europe.

practice.q: Which is the **largest freshwater lake** in the world by area?
practice.solution: **Lake Superior** (USA-Canada) is the largest freshwater lake by area; Baikal is the **deepest**; the Caspian is the largest lake overall but salty.

practice.q: Angel Falls, the highest waterfall in the world, is located in:
practice.solution: **Angel Falls** (about 979 m) drops from the Auyan-tepui tableland in **Venezuela**.

practice.q: The lowest point of the Earth's land surface is:
practice.solution: The **Dead Sea** shore (Israel-Jordan) lies about **430 m below sea level** - the lowest land on Earth; its water is also the saltiest of lakes.

practice.q: Which continent is the largest by area?
practice.solution: **Asia** (about 44 million sq km) is the largest continent, with Africa second and Australia the smallest.

practice.q: The Blue Nile and the White Nile meet at:
practice.solution: They join at **Khartoum** (Sudan); the Blue Nile comes from Lake Tana in Ethiopia and carries most of the flood water.

practice.q: The fjord coast, carved by glaciers into deep sea inlets, is a typical feature of:
practice.solution: **Norway's** west coast is the classic land of **fjords**. The Volga is Europe's longest river; the Danube crosses the most countries.

practice.q: Which continent is **completely covered** in the statements: (1) no permanent population, (2) about 98% under an ice sheet?
practice.solution: **Antarctica** - scientists stay temporarily at research stations (India: Dakshin Gangotri, Maitri, Bharati); it is the coldest continent (Vostok, about -89 C).

practice.q: The Great Dividing Range and the Murray-Darling basin are features of:
practice.solution: The **Great Dividing Range** runs along Australia's east coast; the Murray-Darling is its chief river system. Uluru (Ayers Rock) lies in the centre.

practice.q: The temperate grasslands of **North America** are called:
practice.solution: **Prairies** - North America (wheat belt of Canada-USA). Pampas - Argentina; Steppes - Eurasia; Veld - South Africa.

practice.q: The **Pampas** grasslands, famous for wheat and beef cattle, lie in:
practice.solution: The **Pampas** of Argentina (and Uruguay) are among the world's great farm lands; Buenos Aires stands on their edge.

practice.q:
Match the grassland with its continent:
1. Llanos  2. Campos  3. Canterbury
(i) New Zealand (ii) Venezuela (iii) Brazil
practice.solution: **Llanos** - Venezuela (Orinoco), **Campos** - Brazil, **Canterbury** - New Zealand. All three are tropical (or southern temperate) grasslands.

practice.q: The **Inuit (Eskimos)** traditionally live in the:
options: Arctic regions of North America and Greenland
practice.solution: The **Inuit** are the indigenous people of the Arctic (Alaska, Canada, Greenland); the igloo and the kayak belong to their culture.

practice.q: The **Pygmies**, known as forest dwellers of short stature, live in the:
practice.solution: **Pygmies** - equatorial rainforests of the **Congo basin**. Bushmen - Kalahari; Masai - East African savanna; Tuaregs - Sahara.

practice.q: The **Lapps** (Sami), traditional reindeer herders, are found in:
practice.solution: The **Lapps** live in northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and the Kola peninsula; the Kirghiz are their steppe counterparts in Central Asia.

practice.q: Which country operates the Indian Antarctic research stations **Maitri** and **Bharati**?
practice.solution: **India** runs **Maitri** and **Bharati** (and the earlier, now-buried **Dakshin Gangotri**) - its first expedition reached Antarctica in 1981-82.

practice.q: The **Arctic** is different from Antarctica mainly because the Arctic is:
practice.solution: The Arctic is a **frozen ocean** ringed by the lands of North America, Europe and Asia; **Antarctica is land** ringed by the Southern Ocean.

practice.q: Which country is known as the 'Land of the Rising Sun'?
practice.solution: **Japan** - Nippon, 'origin of the sun', from its position east of the Asian mainland; its flag shows the sun disc.

practice.q: Which country is called the 'Land of a Thousand Lakes'?
practice.solution: **Finland** actually has about 1.88 lakh lakes; Canada has more lakes overall but Finland owns the nickname.

practice.q: The 'Land of the White Elephant' is:
practice.solution: **Thailand** - the white elephant was a royal symbol; it appears on the old flag. Bhutan is the 'Thunder Dragon' land.

practice.q: Which country is called the 'Land of the Midnight Sun' because summer days never fully end in its north?
practice.solution: **Norway** - north of the Arctic Circle the summer Sun never sets. Iceland is 'Fire and Ice'; Ireland the 'Emerald Isle'.

practice.q: Which city is called the 'Eternal City'?
practice.solution: **Rome** - also the 'City of Seven Hills'; Athens is the 'City of Violet Crowns' in older literature.

practice.q: The 'Windy City', famous for its strong lake breezes, is:
practice.solution: **Chicago**, on Lake Michigan, is the Windy City; New York is the Big Apple; San Francisco the Golden Gate City.

practice.q: Johannesburg, the centre of a great mining region, is called the:
practice.solution: **Johannesburg** grew on the Witwatersrand **gold** reefs. Kimberley, not Johannesburg, is linked with diamonds.

practice.q: The Radcliffe Line (1947) is the boundary between:
practice.solution: The **Radcliffe Line** was drawn in **1947** at Partition between India and (West) Pakistan; the Durand Line (1893) separates Pakistan and Afghanistan.

practice.q: The **38th Parallel** is associated with the boundary between:
practice.solution: The **38th Parallel** divides the two Koreas (armistice line, 1953). The 17th Parallel divided Vietnam; the 49th Parallel runs along much of the US-Canada border.

practice.q: The Maginot Line, a chain of concrete fortifications of the 1930s, was built by which country on its border with Germany?
practice.solution: **France** built the **Maginot Line**; German forces simply went around it in 1940. The Hindenburg Line was Germany's own WW1 defence line.

practice.q: Which of the following is correctly matched?
practice.solution: The **Oder-Neisse Line** runs along the Oder and Neisse rivers between Germany and Poland. Durand - Pak-Afghan; McMahon - India-China; Mannerheim - Finland-Russia.

practice.q: 'Ceylon' was the former name of which country?
practice.solution: **Ceylon** became **Sri Lanka** in **1972** when it became a republic; its capital is Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte (Colombo is the commercial hub).

practice.q: The city once called **Constantinople** is today known as:
practice.solution: **Constantinople** was renamed **Istanbul** (officially from 1930); Ankara is Turkey's capital. Peking-Beijing and Rangoon-Yangon are parallel cases.

practice.q: 'Gold Coast', a former British colony, is the old name of which country?
practice.solution: **Gold Coast** became **Ghana** at independence in **1957** - the first sub-Saharan colony to gain freedom. Rhodesia became Zimbabwe (1980).

practice.q: Baghdad, the capital of Iraq, stands on the bank of which river?
practice.solution: **Baghdad - Tigris.** Cairo stands on the Nile; Khartoum at the Blue-White Nile confluence.

practice.q: The capital of Egypt, Cairo, is situated on which river?
practice.solution: **Cairo - Nile**; Egypt itself is the 'Gift of the Nile'.

practice.q: Which of the following capital-river pairs is **wrong**?
practice.solution: **Berlin stands on the Spree** (and the Havel); the Rhine flows through Cologne and Rotterdam, not a capital.

practice.q: Bangkok, the capital of Thailand, lies on which river?
practice.solution: **Bangkok - Chao Phraya** ('River of Kings'). Hanoi - Red River; Dhaka - Buriganga; Yangon - Yangon river.

practice.q: Which single European river flows through the greatest number of capital cities?
practice.solution: The **Danube** passes through **Vienna (Austria), Bratislava (Slovakia), Budapest (Hungary) and Belgrade (Serbia)** - four capitals; the Volga is Europe's longest river but has no capital on it.
